doc.title: Chuck Mancuso interviewed by Monk Rowe, Buffalo, New York, October 10, 2013

title: Paul Whiteman, Ellington and who owns jazz
summary: Mancuso defends Whiteman against critics, contrasts him with Ellington, rejects the idea that blacks own jazz, and explains his teaching aims.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: What about the opposite. Is there someone that comes to mind that you think had minimal talent or individuality but managed to really be at the top of the record charts?

Well Paul Whiteman got a raw deal I thought, you know, the “King of Jazz.” I thought they treated him, a reverse discrimination. Because that’s not answering your question, but they treated him poorly. Because he had great jazz players in his group and he had two things answered. I always have my students take a look at Duke Ellington and Paul Whiteman. And one of the things that my book is trying to show is objectivity. You know Whiteman didn’t stretch to do what Ellington did. And Ellington didn’t get quite the popularity that Paul Whiteman did. But the critics, especially the jazz people, took these rotten shots at him, Whiteman, as in white man robbing the world of jazz. And this idea that blacks own jazz — nobody owns jazz, you know. Most of the players got — because if you’re going to say that then these black men should not be able to play classical music. If you’re going to use that —
I mean that’s pretty ridiculous, isn’t it.

Of course. And it’s nasty thinking number one, and it’s limited thinking number two. And one of the things I’ve tried to show in our world is that, you know I told the class, now we’re going to go to country and folk. Now for many of you, you’re from the northeast, and you’re going to think this stuff is not so great. But I want to show you some really great artists, and today they are treated that way. But they weren’t during their lifetime. And it took a while for some of the younger historians to come in, like the Greil Marcuses, like the Nick Toshes, like the Peter Guralnicks, to really show — now my mentor was doing it. That’s why I’m lucky. So I came up with him and I learned about it. I didn’t really have an opinion, I just didn’t listen to it. And once he got me there and we talked about it all the time, I’d go, what a great man. What a gentle spirit, to not be so obnoxious as this stuff sucks and this stuff is — so that’s what that book tries to just show the people, and you don’t have to like the stuff. And I tell the students, I said, you don’t have to know all those charts. I didn’t write a textbook. I wrote a source book. So it just shows you the enormity of this stuff. And I’m always fascinated by how much was out there.
